Notes · AI film

Routing a script to finished shots across ten AI providers

An AI film pipeline fails in more ways than a traditional one, and almost none of them look like the demo. A shot can come back technically perfect and narratively wrong. These are the notes from building Ghan Cinematic so that each stage can be retried independently instead of re-running the whole film.

The failure is never the same twice

In a render farm, a frame either renders or it does not. In a pipeline routed across ten providers, the failure modes are much less tidy: a provider is down, a prompt returns an empty string, a model drifts the character's face, a video call times out at forty seconds, a keyframe comes back with six fingers.

The consequence is architectural. A pipeline that assumes the happy path will produce a film that works until the first unusual shot, and then stop. The pipeline has to treat every stage as something that can fail independently and be retried without discarding the work already done.

Identity is the hard part, not the resolution

The obvious problem with AI-generated characters is that they are not consistent between shots. The less obvious problem is that they are not consistent enough — a face that changes subtly every shot reads as a different character only if you are paying attention, but it still costs the viewer trust.

  • Lock the identity before the motion. A keyframe per character per lighting state, generated once and reused, beats a fresh generation per shot.
  • Describe the character once, reference everywhere. The description lives in one place; every shot inherits it.
  • Validate before accepting. An asset that fails the identity check is rejected and regenerated, not patched later.

Retry is a design decision

Retrying is where a naive pipeline burns its budget. Three retries per stage sounds reasonable until you have forty shots and four stages. The useful distinction is between a retry that can help and one that cannot:

  • Worth retrying: a provider timeout, an empty response, a rate limit. The same request may well succeed.
  • Not worth retrying: a prompt that returns the wrong subject. The same prompt will keep returning the wrong subject.

That means the retry loop has to be per-stage and per-cause, and the budget has to be tracked per shot rather than per film. Otherwise the cheapest shots pay for the most expensive ones.

Cost is per shot, not per film

When a shot can be generated by a local model or a cloud API, the decision is not "which is better" but "which is cheaper at this shot's requirements". A dialogue close-up wants the best available model. A wide establishing shot with motion does not.

Routing on the shot's actual requirements — resolution, motion, character prominence, how long the shot is on screen — is what makes a ten-provider pipeline practical instead of a ten-provider bill.

The project

Ghan Cinematic is an end-to-end AI film studio: script to shot breakdown to identity-locked characters to video, routed across local GPU models and cloud APIs, with every asset validated before it is accepted.
